deep.reconstruction:
This folio is the opening page of Riemann's fragment XXI, 'Zwei allgemeine Sätze über lineäre Differentialgleichungen mit algebraischen Coefficienten', dated 20 Feb 1857. It was printed in the Nachlass section of Riemann's Gesammelte Werke (1876). The pencil note 'H. Weber geschrieben' indicates the sheet is in Weber's hand, i.e. a copy. The page contains no computations, only a conceptual setup in four steps.

(1) Recalled fact. Consider a homogeneous linear ODE L y = y^(n) + p_1(x) y^(n-1) + ... + p_n(x) y = 0. Every solution is a constant-coefficient combination y = sum c_i y_i of n linearly independent particular solutions y_1..y_n.

(2) Rational coefficients. If the p_k lie in C(x), solutions are in general many-valued. Cut the plane along a suitable system of lines through the singular points. Then each branch of any solution is a constant-coefficient combination of n functions that are single-valued on the cut plane and discontinuous only along the cuts.

(3) Algebraic coefficients. Now let p_k lie in C(x, s), where s is a mu-valued algebraic function of x. Each branch s_j of s gives an equation with its own fundamental system of n solutions. So a branch of a solution is a linear expression in at most mu*n single-valued (cut-plane) functions, of which only the n belonging to one 'group' (one branch of s) actually occur.

(4) Inhomogeneous equations. Riemann notes that L y = f can be made homogeneous of order n+1. Implicitly (my filling): d/dx (L y / f) = 0, i.e. f*(L y)' - f'*(L y) = 0, whose coefficients stay in the same algebraic function field. Hence the theorems to come cover all linear ODEs with algebraic coefficients.

(5) Abstract setup, independent of any ODE.
- Let y_1..y_n be functions of x that are single-valued and finite for all complex x except the branch points a, b, c, ..., g.
- A loop of x around any one of these points sends the vector (y) to a constant linear transformation of itself; these are the local monodromy matrices.
- To normalise, split the sphere into two regions by a closed curve passing successively through all branch points (in the inserted order g, ..., c, b, a).
- In each region the functions are single-valued and continuous; their values in the region on the positive side of the curve are taken as given.
- The next page continues by defining the matrices (A), ..., (G), proving the product relation (G)(F)...(B)(A) = 1, introducing the symbol Q(a..g; A..G; x) and the notion of a class (fixed branch points and monodromy), and diagonalising (A).

In modern terms, this page sets up a vector-valued function on P^1 minus {a, ..., g} with a prescribed monodromy representation of the fundamental group. This is the starting point of what became the Riemann–Hilbert problem (Hilbert's 21st problem).
errors: No mathematical errors on this page.
The phrase 'höchstens mu n' is correct; it is an upper bound because branches of the algebraic function may coincide on degenerate components.

The remark that every inhomogeneous equation is 'easily' made homogeneous of the next order is correct (divide by the right-hand side and differentiate), as long as the right-hand side f is in the same algebraic function field.

results.what: General solution of a homogeneous linear ODE is a constant-coefficient combination of n independent solutions
results.modern_name: Fundamental system / solution space is n-dimensional
results.usually_credited_to: Lagrange, Cauchy; in complex domain Fuchs (1866)

results.what: Branches of solutions with rational/algebraic coefficients are expressed through single-valued functions on a cut plane (at most mu*n of them)
results.modern_name: Single-valued branches on a simply connected cut domain; analytic continuation / monodromy
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann (1857 P-function paper and this Nachlass fragment)

results.what: Reduction of an inhomogeneous linear ODE to a homogeneous one of order n+1
Abstract definition of an n-tuple of functions with prescribed branch points and linear monodromy substitutions, normalised by a closed curve through all branch points
results.modern_name: Monodromy representation; setup of the Riemann–Hilbert problem
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann 1857 (published 1876), later Fuchs, Schlesinger, Hilbert's 21st problem (1900)

deep.surprise_reason: This is the well-known, published (Werke 1876) Riemann fragment that historians already cite as the origin of the Riemann–Hilbert problem. This page holds only its introductory setup, so nothing here is new.

checkable.sympy: x=symbols('x'); L=lambda y: diff(y,x,2)+y; M=lambda y: x*diff(L(y),x)-L(y); [simplify(M(f)) for f in (sin(x),cos(x),x)]
checkable.asserts: Homogenisation of y''+y=x into x*(y'''+y')-(y''+y)=0: all three of sin x, cos x, x solve the order-3 homogeneous equation (each result is 0).
x^a solves the first-order equation x y' = a y (result 0). Its monodromy around 0 is multiplication by exp(2*pi*I*a), the simplest example of a loop acting as a constant linear substitution.
